extracted.intended_audience: students of introductory real analysis or rigorous calculus (advanced high-school to undergraduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory textbook treatment of the construction and properties of number systems: natural, integer, rational, and real numbers; decimal expansions; limits and infinite series; geometric interpretation on the number line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of rational numbers (fractions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When m and n are natural numbers, the symbol m/n is called a rational number. A sub-unit obtained by dividing the original unit 1 into n equal parts is denoted by 1/n; if a given quantity contains exactly m of these sub-units, its measure is denoted by m/n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat m/n as a pure number (divested from measuring context). Addition, multiplication, and equality for these symbols must be defined so they obey the same algebraic laws as natural numbers; definitions are 'forced upon us' by the measuring interpretation. Example notation: m:n sometimes used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic laws preserved in extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental laws of arithmetic (commutative and associative laws of addition and multiplication, and distributive law) that hold for natural numbers continue to hold for rational numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists these explicitly (commutative of addition, associative of addition, commutative of multiplication, associative of multiplication, distributive law). Proofs show these follow from the definitions for fractions; e.g., commutativity of addition for fractions is shown by cross-multiplying numerators/denominators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of operations on fractions are conventional but constrained
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for addition, multiplication, and equality of rational-number symbols are established by definition and chosen for consistency and usefulness; alternative arbitrary rules are logically possible but would be useless for measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the anti-pattern: whimsically defining addition so that 1/2 + 1/2 = 2/4 would be meaningless for measuring. Choose definitions to preserve known arithmetic laws and applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of generalization (extension preserving laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending a domain by introducing new symbols so that the laws that hold in the original domain continue to hold in the larger domain is a characteristic mathematical process of generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: extending from naturals to integers and rationals so subtraction and division become unrestricted (except division by zero). New symbols (0, negative integers, fractions) must have operations defined to preserve existing laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure and field property
rubrics_metrics.description: The rational numbers form a closed domain (a field) in which the rational operations — addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division (except by zero) — may be performed without leaving the domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is why extending to rationals removes restrictions on solving equations a + x = b and ax = b. The domain is explicitly identified as a 'field'; later chapters discuss other fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity to define negatives and zero to allow unrestricted subtraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing 0 and negative integers (…,-2,-1) allows subtraction to be performed without restriction in the extended arithmetic; definitions (e.g., b - a = - (a - b) for b < a) must preserve distributive law and other arithmetic properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example consequence: defining (-1)(-1)=1 follows from wanting distributivity to hold; anti-patterns (defining it as -1) would contradict distributivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of division by zero
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions like 1/0, 3/0, 0/0 are meaningless; division by 0 is excluded because allowing it leads to absurdities (e.g., from 0·1 = 0·2 one would deduce 1 = 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infinity (∞) may be used informally to denote 'unbounded' quantities but must not be treated like ordinary numbers; do not operate with ∞ as though ordinary arithmetic applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical interpretation of numbers on the number axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate points on a straight line (the number axis) with numbers: mark off 0 to 1 as the unit, represent positive numbers to the right and negatives to the left; subdividing the unit into n equal parts represents fractions with denominator n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subdivisions are performed for every integer n, all rational numbers are represented as points on the axis. This gives an intuitive ordering and geometric meaning to arithmetic comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order relation via geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Define A < B for rationals by the geometric fact that the point A lies to the left of B; equivalently, A < B iff B - A is positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves the geometric order when extending arithmetical relations from naturals to rationals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute value properties and triangle inequality for rationals
rubrics_metrics.description: For rational A, |A| = A if A ≥ 0, and |A| = -A if A < 0. If A and B have the same sign then |A + B| = |A| + |B|; if opposite signs then |A + B| < |A| + |B|, leading to the general inequality |A + B| ≤ |A| + |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These basic inequalities are presented as fundamental facts that hold for rationals and are useful in limit arguments later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density of rational points
rubrics_metrics.description: The rational points are dense on the line: within each interval, however small, there exist rational points; in any interval there are infinitely many rationals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: choose denominator n large enough so that 1/n is smaller than the interval length; then some fraction m/n lies inside. This demonstrates there is no interval free of rationals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of incommensurable segments (irrationals exist)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are segments not commensurable with the unit; example: diagonal of a square has length √2 which cannot be expressed as a rational p/q (proof by parity contradiction). Hence irrational numbers must be introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The discovery that rationals are dense but do not cover the line motivates introducing irrationals to maintain correspondence between numbers and points. The diagonal/square proof is the canonical example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decimal fractions and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decimal fractions (finite decimals) represent numbers of the form p/10^n. Any finite decimal with n digits after the point equals an integer divided by 10^n; conversely, rationals whose reduced denominators do not divide a power of 10 cannot be finite decimals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 0.2 = 1/5, 0.004 = 4/1000. Some rationals (e.g., 3/5) are finite decimals, others are not (e.g., 3/35), and those produce infinite periodic decimals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite decimals as limits via nested decimal intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: A point P not represented by a finite decimal is approximated by nested decimal intervals: successive decimal digits determine intervals of length 10^-n that contain P; the infinite decimal z.a1a2a3... represents the unique point contained in every such interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes how one constructs an infinite decimal expansion by iterative subdivision. Example: 0.333... represents 1 as the limit of 0.3, 0.33, 0.333, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept of limit and infinite series as shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: An expression like 1 = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... is shorthand for '1 is the limit of the finite sums s_n as n → ∞'; the infinite enters only as an unending procedure, not an actual completed quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise limit notation (s_n → 1 as n → ∞). Avoid treating ∞ as a number; interpret infinite sums via limits of partial sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of geometric series for |q| < 1
rubrics_metrics.description: For |q| < 1, the infinite geometric series 1 + q + q^2 + q^3 + ... converges to 1/(1 - q); equivalently q^n → 0 as n → ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: use finite sum formula s_n = (1 - q^(n+1))/(1 - q) and let n → ∞. Examples: q = 1/10 gives decimal expansions (0.999... = 1). If |q| ≥ 1 the series does not converge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic decimal expansions characterize rationals
rubrics_metrics.description: The decimal expansion of any rational number is eventually periodic: long division remainders are integers between 1 and q-1, so some remainder repeats within q−1 steps causing a repeating block of digits. Conversely every periodic decimal is rational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1/6 = 0.16666..., 1/7 = 0.142857142857...; finite decimals can be viewed as periodic with trailing zeros. Proof of converse uses geometric series summation of the repeating block.

rubrics_metrics.name: General definition of real numbers by nested intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the continuum (real numbers) as the totality of points corresponding to all sequences of nested intervals with rational endpoints whose lengths tend to zero; postulate that each such nested sequence contains precisely one point on the number axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation detaches the definition from base-10 decimals and yields a base-independent construction. It also justifies calling infinite decimals 'numbers' via correspondence with nested rational intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness and existence postulate for nested-interval point
rubrics_metrics.description: There cannot be more than one point common to all intervals of a nested sequence (because lengths → 0), and geometry postulates that there is exactly one such point; this justifies treating nested sequences as defining real numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From a formal perspective one can treat an 'irrational point' as merely the symbol of its defining nested rational intervals. The postulate is taken as an axiom of geometry and foundational for the continuum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical stance: objects as systems of relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical objects are to be regarded not as 'things in themselves' but as entities determined by their mathematical properties and relations; e.g., an irrational point can be defined intrinsically by a nested sequence of rational intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underpins the intrinsic (axiomatic) approach to real numbers: definitions and properties are primary, not any naive concrete existence. It is a methodological criterion for rigorous development.
